candidates.title: Learned lessons on Socially Assistive Robot design in Elderly Care: proposal and insights of a Collaborative Design Framework
candidates.abstract: Abstract Purpose: This paper proposes a co-design framework and evaluates its practical application during a project involving robot deployment in a retirement home.Methods: The study details the hybrid methodology used during a 19-week Socially Assistive Robot deployment involving 17 older adults and 3 professionals in a Spanish retirement home. Robot performance was evaluated via the AUSUS framework, prioritizing techniques designed to minimize participant fatigue.Results: While participants reported high perceived utility, the deployment revealed two distinct obstacles. First, low technical efficacy was primarily driven by inherent unpredictability and daily incidents of a real-world environment, which negatively cascaded into the overall user experience. Second, the study exposed the inherent limitations of traditional User-Centered Design practices, particularly the challenge of defining and sustaining active participant engagement within complex, shared care ecosystems. Conclusion: Driven by the lessons learned from the CAMPERO project, the paper underscores the necessity for contextual pre-assessments, active participant empowerment, and pragmatic evaluation scoping. Ultimately, these insights provide a critical foundation for future methodological advancements, ensuring SAR deployments are genuinely collaborative, needs-driven, methodologically responsible and integrated without disrupting the care ecosystem.

candidates.title: GVT3D: Gesture-Vision-Text Token Enrichment for 3D Embodied Reference Understanding
candidates.abstract: Natural human-robot interaction requires robots to interpret language and gestures within a 3D environment to support tasks such as pick-and-place and object retrieval. 3D Embodied Reference Understanding (3D-ERU) supports this by identifying the 3D location of a target object from a scene (point-cloud) containing a human pointing gesture and an accompanying language description. However, current 3D-ERU models lack alignment of cross-modal representations and incur high processing costs that increase with the point-cloud's size. To address this, we propose GVT3D, which employs an Embodied Fusion module that jointly models language, gesture, and vision inputs within a shared embedding space, promoting cross-modal alignment. We additionally introduce a foveation approach that selectively processes the point cloud within a coarse region around the estimated pointing direction to reduce computations. GVT3D achieves ~8% higher accuracy and foveation enables 2.95x faster execution while maintaining comparable accuracy, relative to prior 3D-ERU models.

candidates.title: VagueBench: Benchmarking the Robustness of Embodied Agents on Ambient Context Illusions
candidates.abstract: Embodied agents are increasingly deployed in open-world environments, yet current robustness evaluations remain biased toward hazardous instructions and jailbreak vulnerabilities. A more fundamental issue is largely overlooked: agents are rarely tested under semantically sufficient but contextually minimal instructions (i.e., common in real-world human communication), where auxiliary contextual cues are absent. For the first, we identify a novel phenomenon termed Ambient Context Illusion, where agents fail to execute tasks correctly when non-essential contextual details are omitted, despite unchanged task semantics. To systematically study this, we establish VagueBench, a benchmark built upon the AI2-THOR interactive simulation environment for the evaluation of context dependency in embodied agents. We systematically consider key semantic components of instructions (entities, procedures, constraints, and prior knowledge) and derive a unified taxonomy with four categories and nine subtypes to reduce auxiliary information. VagueBench contains 1,303 instruction pairs across diverse indoor environments, constructed via a human-agent co-generation framework that integrates semantic redundancy estimation, taxonomy-guided transformation, and rigorous semantic-invariance verification. Through extensive evaluation on 6 state-of-the-art embodied agents, we observe significant degradation on VagueBench in both task performance and executability (relatively -19.65% in task success rate and relatively +54.10% in empty plan rate) revealing a strong reliance on auxiliary linguistic signals rather than core task semantics. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this phenomenon persists in real-world robotic systems, where it can lead to incorrect decisions and potential safety risks.

candidates.title: TinyML Hits the Memory Wall: A Benchmark of Ten Sub-Watt Edge Devices
candidates.abstract: Neural network inference at the edge must fit tight energy budgets. Existing benchmarks compare few devices, do not report energy on a common basis, and omit the newest microcontrollers with an NPU or the 1 GHz Cortex-M85. Hardware-aware design also ranks networks by MAC count, yet no study has tested whether this proxy holds across accelerators. We benchmark sub-watt edge AI hardware by evaluating four CNNs (MobileNetV3, MCUNetV1, EfficientNet, SqueezeNet) and two tiny transformers (MobileViT-XXS, DeiT-tiny) on ten commercial devices: an in-sensor DSP (Sony IMX500), four MCUs with an NPU (STM32N6, Alif Ensemble E7/E8, GreenWaves GAP9), and five MCUs without an NPU (STM32U5, Apollo510B, ESP32-S3 Xtensa LX7, RA8M2, STM32V8). Four devices are novel (Alif E8, Apollo510B, RA8M2, STM32V8). Measured as energy above idle, the IMX500 (0.13-0.35 mJ) uses 1.3-3x less energy than the STM32N6 (0.31-1.05 mJ) on every model; the GAP9 uses the least on MobileNetV3 and the Alif E7 the least on MCUNetV1 and SqueezeNet. All four use 6-34x less energy than the STM32V8 (1.85-3.98 mJ), and the Alif E7 and IMX500 form the power-performance Pareto front. Latency on all four accelerators scales with memory traffic (bytes of weights and activations, r >= 0.98) and not with MACs, so they are memory-bound, while no MCU without an NPU is. The NPU advantage grows with intensity from 1.4x over a 1 GHz Cortex-M85 on MCUNetV1 to 8.2x on SqueezeNet. MAC count is therefore a misleading cost proxy for sub-watt accelerators.

candidates.title: Understanding Human-Robot Collaboration through Joint Action
candidates.abstract: Human-robot collaboration requires partners to coordinate interdependent contributions toward a shared goal. Joint Action theory provides concepts for understanding this coordination, but how these concepts are instantiated and combined across empirical research remains fragmented. We conducted a systematic review following PRISMA 2020, identifying 83 empirical papers published between 2021 and 2026. Through theory-driven framework analysis, we organized the literature into nine constructs across three capacities: Representation, Prediction, and Integration. We analyze how these constructs are distributed and co-occur across studies, revealing where empirical evidence concentrates and where it is absent. By mapping empirical HRC research onto a unified Joint Action framework, this review offers a coherent overview of HRC studies, identifies gaps in current evidence, and provides guidelines for future research.

candidates.title: Whale You Go Green? Immediate and Longitudinal Effects of Embodied Conversational AI Avatars on Sustainable Behavioral Tendencies and Pro-Environmental Attitudes
candidates.abstract: Embodied conversational AI can be persuasive, but can it motivate people to develop sustainable behavioral tendencies and increase pro-environmental attitudes? We conducted a randomized experiment (N = 576) comparing four embodied avatars--a beluga whale, Greta Thunberg, Emma Watson, and a generic human--with a text chatbot and no-intervention control. All embodied conditions increased immediate sustainable product selection relative to the control (beta = .401-.609, all q <= .0126) and chatbot (beta = .398-.604, all q <= .007), without differing significantly from one another. Only the Beluga condition increased immediate pro-environmental attitudes relative to the control after correction. Among 287 returners assessed two months later, following an intermediate assigned-condition session, Beluga also showed significantly higher pre-booster sustainable product choice compared to the control (beta = .657, q = .0176). Although it did not significantly outperform other embodied agents, these findings establish the immediate potential of nonhuman embodied avatar interfaces as a promising direction for memorable environmental interventions.

candidates.title: Embodied Multimedia: From Multimedia Content to Situated Human-AI Interaction
candidates.abstract: Multimedia research, which has traditionally been concerned with the analysis and generation of multimedia content, has increasingly addressed multimodal human behavior. This development is exemplified by current ACM Multimedia Challenges, including POLY-SIM [3], which addresses robust speaker identification under missing-modality and cross-lingual scenarios, MultiMediate [2], which targets engagement estimation across domain, age, and culture, and REACT [4], which focuses on generating appropriate facial reactions in dyadic interactions. Together, these challenges reflect a broader shift from analyzing multimedia content toward analyzing, understanding and generating multimodal behavior in increasingly complex social contexts. The next frontier is to develop embodied AI systems that understand, support, and fluently participate in situated human interaction. We pursue this vision through virtual agents and social robots that facilitate communication between people and AI and increasingly between people themselves. The talk will demonstrate how pretrained multimodal foundation models can be leveraged to create context-aware embodied AI. Drawing on applications in assistive communication, AI-mediated group discussions, and social coaching, the talk will illustrate how embodied agents enabled by these models can help overcome communication barriers, facilitate social interaction, and foster authentic self-expression. At the same time, significant challenges remain in grounding multimodal models in physical and social context, ensuring responsive and coordinated behavior, and evaluating whether apparently socially intelligent behavior is appropriate, robust, and trustworthy [1].

candidates.title: Interactions
candidates.abstract: This chapter explores the diverse interaction modalities that are involved in human–robot interaction (HRI) through extended reality (XR). These interactions enable communication and collaboration between humans and robots. It deals with physical and haptic interaction, as well as gesture- and movement-based interaction. Apart from this, it also deals with voice, gaze, and controller-based interfaces. The environmental, spatial, and tangible interactions are also discussed in the context of embodied and situated action. The chapter also addresses multimodal and adaptive interaction strategies that combine multiple input and feedback channels. It also deals with collaborative, social, autonomous, and instruction-based interaction paradigms. This chapter, therefore, deals with selecting and designing interaction modalities that are effective, intuitive, and context-aware within XR-enabled HRI systems.

candidates.title: From virtual pets to AI companions: A relational-design framework for human–artificial bonds
candidates.abstract: Artificial companions occupy a hybrid position between interactive systems and social partners, yet research remains divided across virtual pets, social robots, relational agents, mixed-reality animals, and generative AI companions. This critical integrative review asks which design properties can make sustained human–artificial relationships possible without assuming that relational significance depends on human likeness or technical sophistication. It develops a five-dimensional relational-design framework: temporal continuity; legible need and vulnerability; contingent responsiveness; social presence and anthropomorphic interpretation; and recurrent care and support. A central revision to the framework is that care is not necessarily directed from the human toward the artificial entity. In many relational-agent, health, educational, and companionship contexts, the human is the recipient of support, and the system must detect, interpret, and respond to human needs. The framework therefore treats care as directional and potentially reciprocal, while distinguishing companion relationships from training simulations in which a virtual patient or student is primarily an object of professional practice. Drawing on research in virtual pets, social responses to computers, relational agents, human–robot interaction, digital possessions, and AI companions, the review connects each dimension to identifiable literature and illustrates its operation across different system types. It also examines well-being, asymmetrical power, vulnerable populations, loss, and platform governance. The framework is a conceptual tool rather than a validated measurement instrument; its value lies in generating comparative hypotheses and design questions that can be tested longitudinally and across contexts.

candidates.title: Performance and moral trust in care robotics: ethical foundations for human–robot relationships
candidates.abstract: Abstract As global populations age and birth rates decline, many societies, especially in developed countries, face critical labor shortages in the caregiving sector. This demographic imbalance is straining existing care infrastructures and raising urgent questions about how to support an increasing number of elderly individuals who can no longer live independently. Socially interactive AI systems, particularly care robots, have emerged as a promising technological response. However, their successful integration into real-world care settings hinges on more than technical capability; it requires appropriately calibrated reliance on robotic performance and morally trustworthy sociotechnical care arrangements. This paper investigates the ethical and conceptual foundations of trust in human–robot interactions, with a focus on the caregiving context. Building on the distinction between performance trust and moral trust, we argue that its application to care robotics reveals an agency-trust mismatch: care robots are not moral agents, yet care contexts generate morally significant expectations concerning dignity, autonomy, privacy, non-deception, responsibility, and well-being. We therefore reconceptualize moral trust in care robotics as sociotechnical moral trust, directed not toward the robot alone but toward the broader care arrangement in which robotic behavior is designed, deployed, monitored, governed, and corrected by human and institutional actors. On this basis, we distinguish robot-level performance trust from system-level moral trustworthiness and derive ethical design and governance principles for trustworthy care-robotic systems.

candidates.title: Social Structural Pressures and East Asian Adolescents' Consumption Behaviors Toward Virtual Anime-Style Characters: The Mediating Role of Parasocial Attachment
candidates.abstract: East Asian adolescents face multiple structural stressors, including academic pressure, peer competition, parental expectations, and uncertainty about the future. When these pressures frustrate their basic psychological needs, some turn to virtual anime-style games for emotional compensation, forming parasocial attachments to virtual characters. Integrating compensatory consumption theory and parasocial relationship theory, this paper synthesizes existing literature to construct an analytical pathway from structural social stress through psychological need deficits and parasocial attachment to consumption behavior. The analysis suggests that when academic competition and family expectations leave adolescents' needs for belongingness and competence unfulfilled, their emotional involvement with virtual characters accelerates from casual contact toward attachment; once attachment is formed, consumption becomes a natural extension of maintaining and expressing the relationship, manifested both in the general logic of paying for parasocial proximity and in possessiveness-driven consumption that transforms intangible bonds into tangible possessions. Moreover, the developmental asynchrony between the socioemotional system and the cognitive control system during adolescence further heightens adolescents' susceptibility to immediate rewards in gaming contexts. By integrating compensatory consumption theory and parasocial relationship theory within the novel context of anime-style virtual games, this study extends the application boundaries of both frameworks, and suggests that parents and schools should attend to the real-world satisfaction of adolescents' needs for autonomy, competence, and belonging rather than merely restricting gaming time and spending.

candidates.title: CEMIR vs. FISER: a comparative study of reasoning-based and enrichment-based approaches to pragmatic intent recognition
candidates.abstract: Intent recognition in human-robot interaction requires agents to resolve ambiguous natural language instructions by inferring the speaker's underlying goals. Research has increasingly focused on two notable paradigms for addressing this task: structured symbolic reasoning and multimodal input enrichment. However, it remains unclear whether enrichment-based methods provide benefit in settings where the ambiguity concerns unstated human intent rather than missing observable scene information. In this paper, we present a comparative and diagnostic study benchmarking FISER - a framework utilizing structured social and embodied reasoning - against CEMIR (Context-Enriched Multimodal Intent Recognition), a method that performs multimodal enrichment by synthesizing narratives and photorealistic images from textual prompts. By evaluating both approaches across four Large Language Models (LLMs), ranging from Qwen2.5-Omni-3B to GPT-5, on the HandMeThat v2 benchmark, we analyze their capability to resolve pragmatic ambiguities. Our statistical analysis, employing multiple-comparison correction, reveals no statistically significant difference in performance between FISER and CEMIR across any model or difficulty level. This pattern holds across all sixteen model-by-difficulty comparisons, as well as in a targeted ablation isolating CEMIR's narrative and visual components. Instead, performance is primarily associated with backbone capability and the inherent difficulty of the ambiguity. These findings suggest a boundary condition for text-derived multimodal enrichment: when the relevant task constraints are already available in the textual instruction, synthetic multimodal augmentation may not provide measurable benefit over structured reasoning on the same text.

candidates.title: Conditions and Pathways for Integrating Smart Care Robots Into Long-Term Care Facilities: Qualitative Study From Nursing Assistants’ Perspectives
candidates.abstract: Background: Smart care robots are increasingly viewed as a potential way to address care burden and support care quality in long-term care facilities. However, their integration into routine care practice remains limited, and the conditions required for their effective implementation are not yet well understood from the perspective of frontline nursing assistants. Objective: This study aimed to clarify nursing assistants' core functional expectations of smart care robots in long-term care facilities and to explore the key conditions for their integration into practice. Methods: A qualitative descriptive study was conducted. Using purposive sampling, 31 frontline nursing assistants were recruited from 5 long-term care facilities in Chengdu, Sichuan Province, China, with recruitment assistance from facility administrators and eligibility screening by the research team. Semistructured face-to-face interviews were conducted between September and November 2025. Data were analyzed using framework analysis. Results: Framework analysis produced 4 analytical domains: real-world care needs, limited facilitating conditions, major anticipated barriers, and preparatory pathways for implementation. Participants expected robots to support safety monitoring and risk warning, standardized checking and management, repetitive physical tasks, and basic interaction. Although some openness to technology and organizational support existed, these facilitating conditions were insufficient for routine implementation. Key barriers included unclear human-robot collaboration models, inadequate organizational capacity, potential new care risks, and weak external support. Participants emphasized organizational assessment, contextual adaptation, pilot testing, and structured training as essential preparatory steps. Emotional support functions were also valued for alleviating caregivers' emotional burden in high-intensity care work. Conclusions: Openness to technology, supportive organizational climates, and positive policy and social signals provided an initial foundation for considering robot integration. However, uncertainties remained around human-robot collaboration, risk management, organizational capacity, and concrete external support. Organizational assessment, contextual adaptation, real-world pilot testing, and practical training warrant further evaluation before wider implementation.

candidates.title: Security and Privacy‐Preserving Tiny Machine Learning
candidates.abstract: This work examines the privacy and security issues with tiny machine learning (TinyML) and proposes potential solutions to improve dependability and trust in practical applications. A thorough analysis of current security risks is conducted, including data leakage, model extraction, and adversarial assaults. Furthermore, their suitability for TinyML environments is examined for privacy-preserving strategies, including secure enclaves, federated learning, and differential privacy. Because of their limited resources, TinyML systems present particular security and privacy issues that reduce the efficacy of conventional defences. New approaches to reducing these concerns, like decentralized learning, safe model deployment, and lightweight encryption, appear promising. This study offers a thorough examination of privacy and security concerns unique to TinyML, a comparatively unexplored subject within the larger field of artificial intelligence (AI) security. It advances secure edge AI research by bridging the gap between TinyML restrictions and contemporary security solutions.

candidates.title: Dancing with REEM-C: A Robot-To-Human Physical-Social Communication Study
candidates.abstract: Humans often work closely together and relay a wealth of information through physical interaction. Robots, on the other hand, are not yet able to work similarly closely with humans and to effectively convey information when engaging in physical-social human-robot interaction (psHRI). This currently limits the potential of human-robot collaboration to solve real-world problems. This paper investigates how to establish clear and intuitive robot-to-human communication, while considering human comfort during psHRI. We approach this question from the perspective of a leader-follower dancing scenario, in which a full-body humanoid robot leads a human by signaling the next steps through a choice of communication modalities including haptic, visual, and audio signals. This is achieved through the development of a split whole-body control framework combining admittance and impedance control on the upper body, with position control on the lower body for balancing and stepping. Robot-led psHRI participant experiments allowed us to verify controller performance, as well as to build an understanding of what types of communication work better from the perspective of human partners, particularly in terms of perceived effectiveness and comfort.

candidates.title: Children’s Engagement during Cognitive Assessments with Minimal Robot Intervention
candidates.abstract: Standard pediatric cognitive and projective assessments can be monotonous and provoke anxiety. This reduces children's engagement and compliance and diminishes the quality of observable behavior. In this work, we present a workflow that transfers routine paper-and-pencil tasks to a tablet application and adds a NAO humanoid robot as a social partner. Our goal is to provide a robot-and-tablet system for standardized assessments. In this exploratory study, we focused on quantifying the added contribution of the robot to engagement compared to a tablet-only system. To this end, we evaluated the workflow in a pediatric clinic with 24 participants, each with a distinct neurodevelopmental disorder diagnosis, using a controlled, between-subjects design. The tablet-only condition delivered the same activities and pacing without robot cues. This served as a control to isolate the effect of social scaffolding. Licensed therapists rated engagement using the Pediatric Assessment of Rehabilitation Engagement (PARE) scale. Our preliminary findings suggest that the robot's presence supported higher observable engagement and sustained participation without altering the rapport within the child–therapist–robot triad. Moreover, results in the PARE scale were significantly different between the two conditions when considering the age of the little patients (with mean age 10 vs. 8, respectively). While the small sample size and age distribution warrant cautious interpretation, this work highlights a robot's potential contribution to children's engagement during standardized assessment.

candidates.title: When thanks have nowhere to go: emotional indebtedness in the age of service robots
candidates.abstract: Introduction When hotel service robots deliver meaningful service, customers may experience emotional indebtedness—a moral-emotional state arising from perceived obligation without a clear target for reciprocity. This study examines how social (social presence, enjoyment) and nonsocial (novelty, performance) attributes of service robots influence emotional indebtedness and subsequent brand loyalty. Methods Survey data were collected from 462 hotel guests in China with direct service robot experience. Structural equation modeling (SEM) with maximum likelihood estimation was employed, incorporating second-order latent constructs and multi-group analysis by anthropomorphism level. Results Social attributes significantly increased emotional indebtedness, whereas nonsocial attributes either reduced or failed to elicit such responses. Emotional indebtedness positively predicted brand loyalty. Multi-group analyses revealed that the effect of social attributes on emotional indebtedness was invariant across anthropomorphism levels, whereas anthropomorphism moderated the relationship between nonsocial attributes and emotional indebtedness and the conversion of indebtedness into brand loyalty. Discussion These findings extend social exchange theory to robot-mediated hospitality services, demonstrating that customers’ moral-emotional responses depend more on how robot interactions are socially interpreted than on functional performance alone. Anthropomorphism functions as a selective boundary condition rather than a uniform amplifier of emotional engagement.

candidates.title: Mirror Skin: In Situ Visualization of Robot Touch Intent on Robot Skin
candidates.abstract: Effective communication of robot touch intent is essential for safe and predictable physical human-robot interaction. While intent communication has been widely studied, existing approaches lack the spatial specificity and semantic depth necessary to efficiently convey robot touch intent. We present Mirror Skin, a cephalopod-inspired concept that mirrors in-situ visual representations of a human’s body parts onto the corresponding robot’s touch region to communicate who shall initiate touch, where it will occur, and when it is imminent. We informed the design of Mirror Skin through a structured design exploration with experts and demonstrate the real-world feasibility of Mirror Skin with a proof-of-concept prototype. User studies in VR and with the physical prototype showed that Mirror Skin significantly improves accuracy and response times for interpreting touch intent and improves the user experience during physical human-robot interactions.

candidates.title: RoboMMT: Learning Stable Tracking of Modulated Expressive and Interactive Robot Motion
candidates.abstract: Expressive robot motion can improve naturalness, effectiveness, and perceived likability in human-robot interaction. When deployed on dynamically unstable platforms, however, reactive execution of expressive body motion may bring the robot to its stability limits, especially when expressivity is decoupled from physical control. In this paper, we present RoboMMT (Robot Modulated Motion Tracking), a modular control architecture that couples parameterized expressive motion synthesis, physics-based character control, and reactive adaptation to spatial interaction goals. Our approach trains a reference-conditioned tracking policy across a broad domain of expressivity, enabling it to faithfully realize the commanded motions while maintaining dynamic stability. Goal reactivity is achieved by training lightweight, task-specific interaction policies that modulate the reference generator's spatial goal-attraction point, with the stabilizing tracking policy kept in the loop. Evaluations on a quadruped and two humanoid robots show that the learned tracker remains stable and accurate across the entire modulation domain, whereas trackers trained without this coverage lose balance, tracking accuracy, or both. We show that layering closed-loop goal adaptation over this foundation enables interactive facing and pointing behaviors, while maintaining stable execution and comparable reference-tracking fidelity. The robot learns to proactively redistribute its weight and take corrective steps. Zero-shot sim-to-real transfer is demonstrated through real-robot experiments on a quadruped under heavy disturbances.

candidates.title: Low‐Power Tiny Machine Learning‐Based Animal Sound Classification Using the Sound Classification of Animal Voice
candidates.abstract: One essential use of bioacoustics and AI is the classification of animal sounds, enabling automated species identification, wildlife monitoring, and conservation initiatives. The goal of the proposed system is to use a TinyML-based system for classifying animal sounds via energy-efficient microcontrollers, such as Raspberry Pi Pico or ESP32. We extract important audio features from the Earth Species Library dataset “Sound Classification of Animal Voice,” train a lightweight convolutional neural network (CNN), and optimize it for embedded deployment. Melfrequency cepstral coefficients (MFCCs), which are brief yet informative input features, are created from raw audio files as part of the data preprocessing step of the workflow. After that, a neural network optimized for TinyML is trained to identify various animal sounds, including those of birds, reptiles, amphibians, and mammals. TensorFlow Lite for Microcontrollers (TFLM) is used to deploy the trained model onto edge devices after it has been quantized for INT8 precision and converted to TensorFlow Lite (TFLite) format. This implementation enabled applications in wildlife monitoring, smart farms, conservation technology, and autonomous environmental sensing systems, which shows that real-time, low-power animal sound recognition is feasible.

candidates.title: LEXICAL AND PRAGMATIC FEATURES OF FAN COMMUNICATION ON THE SOCIAL MEDIA PLATFORM X
candidates.abstract: The widespread use of social media has changed the ways in which audiences interact with popular culture, leading to the emergence of online fan communities. An online fandom is examined as a community of people united by a common interest in a particular object of popular culture who actively interact on social media. When fans interact online, they exchange information, express their opinions, emotions, attitudes towards actors, events and other fans, creating a sense of community. Although fan culture has been examined in cultural studies, psychology and media studies, the linguistic organisation of fan communication on social media platforms has received limited scholarly attention. The aim of this article is to study the linguistic characteristics of fandom communication on the X platform (formerly Twitter), with particular attention to its lexical and pragmatic features. The analysis is based on a corpus of posts and comment threads related to popular films, television series and actors. It identifies the main features of fandom communication on social media, including the construction of group identity, the use of linguistic devices to express evaluation and emotion, parasocial relationships between fans and celebrities and the use of intertextual references. The results demonstrate that fandom discourse on X is characterised by lexical innovation, the use of personal pronouns (we, us, our vs. they, them, their) and fandom- specific community labels to establish in-group identity, the frequent use of online slang and evaluative language. Fans reduce the perceived social distance between themselves and celebrities through the use of diminutive forms of address and nicknames. Communication within fandom spaces is also highly intertextual, it relies on shared vocabulary, memes and inside jokes based on common knowledge of films, television series, celebrities and fan culture. This study contributes to current research on online communication and language use on social media platforms.

candidates.title: OpenZilo: An Open Smart-Ring Platform for Human-Centric Sensing and Interaction with Robots
candidates.abstract: Wearable robot interfaces must connect user input to timely physical action. We present the proposed platform, an open smart-ring platform for studying this connection across task stages. The ring integrates a microphone, an inertial measurement unit, photoplethysmography, and skin-temperature sensing. Its software architecture separates acquisition, event interpretation, interaction policy, and robot execution. We characterize seven operating modes and evaluate speech and gesture control with 10 participants. Across five commands and 250 trials per modality, speech and gestures achieved task success rates of 90.4% and 88.8%, respectively. Recognition accuracy exceeded task success for both modalities. Gaussian hidden Markov models achieved higher accuracy than a support vector machine across three vocabulary sizes, with longer scoring times. Following a shared spoken task start, gesture-based adjustments had shorter median response times than speech. Whole-task success was 70.0% with gestures and 64.0% with speech. We further examine physiological-event-triggered robot interaction using simulated event notifications. Mean notification-receipt-to-arrival times were 11.71 s for the robot and 9.20 s for an on-site person. These descriptive findings support evaluating wearable robot interfaces through both recognition and physical outcomes, with timing measures appropriate to each task stage.

candidates.title: Ask to Evolve: A Unified Harness for Lifelong Embodied Navigation with Hybrid Action Space and Persistent Memory
candidates.abstract: Giving embodied agents the freedom to act autonomously, initiate interactions, and understand their surroundings through experience is a step toward bringing them to life in the physical world. Realizing this vision requires action, interaction, and memory to work together, so that each encounter can inform current decisions and contribute experience for future tasks. We present EvoLife, a unified navigation harness that enables a multimodal embodied agent to choose how to move, when to ask, and what experience to carry forward. Its hybrid action space supports waypoint navigation, local discrete adjustments, pixel-based navigation, and object-directed navigation. Active interaction allows the agent to seek clarification or assistance when it encounters ambiguity or difficulty, while persistent spatial memory binds observations and dialogue to places, retaining useful experience to guide subsequent visits. We evaluate eight benchmarks across four task families: vision-language navigation, object navigation, interactive instance navigation, and continuous multi-task navigation. With an average of only 1.87 active interactions per episode, our method achieves a first-visit success rate (SR) of 100% across four 100-episode sets spanning vision-language navigation and object navigation. Complete-sequence SR reaches 98% on 50 LHPR-VLN sequences and 94% on 50 GOAT-Bench sequences. In the R2R revisit setting, success weighted by path length (SPL) increases from 82.23% to 93.31% with retained experience. Multi-day physical navigation further demonstrates exploration, proactive help-seeking, and revisiting remembered places. Together, these results advance the vision of bringing embodied agents to life through autonomous action, proactive interaction, and the accumulation and reuse of experience.

candidates.title: Artificial Intelligence in the Behavioral Health Professions: Ethical and Risk Management Issues. Frederic G. Reamer
candidates.abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) continues to emerge throughout the social work field, considering the ethical implications for the use of AI in the behavioral health field is a necessary task. Reamer, who is recognized as a pioneer in social work ethics, has many years of expertise in developing guides to ethical decision-making, which positions him as the perfect candidate to answer the call to the constantly evolving use of AI in behavioral health and its ethics and risk management issues. His expertise is evident in his application of AI to ethical challenges, the knowledge offered, and the case studies provided. Reamer offers the insight needed to critically reflect on the ethical use of AI in the behavioral health profession. The book is organized into four chapters for a comprehensive exploration of AI use and ethical and risk management issues. The first chapter provides a historical overview of AI and information about the various AI options that can be used in behavioral health settings. Commonly used AI tools—such as chatbots, social robots, search engines, predictive analytics tools, speech-to-text tools, text recognition, speech generation, image recognition and generation, and research tools—are explained. Reamer defines each AI option and presents its benefits and risks. Case studies are used to offer real-world practice experiences. Through the use of case studies, Reamer brings attention to the ethical implications and risks that could impact the individual and the practice. Explored in the book are ethical considerations such as the behavioral health organization’s duty to inform an individual of the risks to privacy when disclosing information to a chatbot offered through the organization or the use of research tools that allow researchers to condense literature or draft research papers. Reamer delves into five ways in which AI is used in behavioral health: (1) providing clinical services, (2) documenting clinical services and encounters, (3) performing administrative tasks and functions, (4) conducting research and program evaluations, and (5) educating, training, and supervising students and practitioners. By understanding the five primary ways AI functions in behavioral health, readers gain the foundation necessary to ensure its ethical and responsible use.

candidates.title: Future Directions in Tiny Machine Learning
candidates.abstract: Tiny machine learning (TinyML) represents a transformative frontier in the evolution of artificial intelligence (AI), merging machine learning capabilities with ultra-low-power embedded systems to enable real-time inference at the edge. As data generation accelerates across billions of Internet of Things (IoT) devices, the need for intelligent edge computing that operates efficiently without relying on cloud infrastructure has become critical. TinyML addresses this demand by enabling localized AI processing on constrained devices with limited memory, computation, and energy resources. This chapter provides a comprehensive exploration of the cutting-edge advancements and research trends shaping the present and future landscape of TinyML. We begin by analyzing the core technological enablers of TinyML, including the rise of energy-efficient microcontrollers, specialized AI hardware accelerators, and neuromorphic computing platforms that emulate human brain-like functionality. Innovations in model compression techniques—such as pruning, quantization, and knowledge distillation—play a central role in shrinking complex deep learning models into formats suitable for resource-constrained environments. Additionally, adopting federated learning architectures allows distributed training and data privacy preservation directly on edge nodes, enabling collaborative intelligence without centralized data aggregation. The chapter also highlights the emergence of event-driven AI, which processes sensory inputs based on relevance or change detection rather than continuous sampling, thus reducing power consumption and latency. These techniques are further enhanced by software frameworks tailored for TinyML deployment, including TensorFlow Lite Micro, Edge Impulse, and TVM. Their integration enables scalable development across various application domains. Real-world implementations of TinyML are explored in depth, with practical use cases spanning healthcare, industrial IoT, agriculture, and smart cities. In healthcare, wearable biosensors powered by TinyML enable continuous physiological monitoring, early disease detection, and personalized health feedback. In industrial environments, TinyML enables predictive maintenance systems that detect anomalies in machinery before catastrophic failures occur. Additionally, autonomous drones and surveillance systems powered by on-device AI offer scalable solutions for crowd analytics, traffic monitoring, and environmental sensing in urban settings. Despite its growing potential, TinyML faces significant challenges, particularly concerning energy constraints, data privacy, and security. To address these issues, emerging solutions such as homomorphic encryption for secure inference, blockchain-based identity management for trusted edge collaboration, and hardware-rooted trust anchors for secure boot processes are examined. Furthermore, the ethical dimensions of deploying AI at the edge—such as algorithmic bias, data ownership, and transparency—are critically assessed. Looking forward, the chapter investigates future research directions and anticipated breakthroughs. The integration of TinyML with 6G-enabled IoT ecosystems is poised to enable intelligent, real-time, and ultra-reliable machine-type communication. Biomedical AI applications powered by TinyML are expected to revolutionize early diagnostics and personalized treatment using implantable or ingestible AI chips. Additionally, advances in cognitive computing and neuromorphic architectures hold promise for self-learning edge devices that adapt dynamically to contextual changes in their environments.

candidates.title: Robotic Security: A Dual-Domain Analysis of Security Robots and Robot Cybersecurity
candidates.abstract: Robotic security operates across two distinct but increasingly converging domains: the deployment of robots as security agents (security robotics) and the protection of robotic systems from cyber-physical attacks (robot cybersecurity). This paper provides a structured examination of both domains. In the first, security robots—including patrol robots, sentry systems, and autonomous surveillance platforms—are analyzed in terms of their applications, capabilities, and the human–robot interaction challenges they pose. In the second, the unique vulnerabilities of robotic systems are examined, including threats to sensors, actuators, communication channels, and the Robot Operating System (ROS) ecosystem, alongside emerging defense mechanisms such as intrusion detection systems and secure-by-design architectures. We complement the review with an empiricalcomponent: a structured survey of N = 48 security-robot deployments, a simulated evaluation of an intrusion-detection pipeline on robotic network traffic collected from a ROS 2 testbed, and asecondary analysis of published human–robot trust data. Results indicate that (i) fewer than one infive deployed security robots incorporate any documented cyber-hardening, and hardening isstatistically decoupled from network exposure; (ii) a univariate-feature-selection IDS retains 99.3% of baseline macro-F1 while reducing feature dimensionality by 74.4% and halving edge inference latency; and (iii) perceived trust in a security robot is predicted more strongly by perceived integrity than by perceived ability. The paper argues that the increasing autonomy and connectivity ofsecurity robots creates a recursive vulnerability: the very systems deployed to provide securitybecome attractive targets for adversarial compromise. A unified perspective that treats roboticsecurity as a cyber-physical problem—rather than two separate fields—is necessary for the safe and trustworthy deployment of security robotics.

candidates.title: When robots malfunction: children’s and teachers’ responses in Korean preschool classrooms
candidates.abstract: This study investigates how children and teachers in Korean preschool classrooms respond to naturally occurring robot malfunctions during interactions with AI-powered humanoid robots. Over a three-month period, two robots were integrated into naturalistic play sessions with five-year-old children. Drawing on lag-1 sequential analysis, the study identified immediate interactional patterns surrounding robot breakdown episodes. Children’s verbal and embodied reactions – such as repetition, adjusted phrasing, name-calling, emotional disengagement, and laughter – suggest that children actively attempted to manage or restore interaction during robot malfunction episodes. These responses indicate that children treated robots as responsive social actors and adjusted their interactional behaviors during breakdown situations. Robot malfunctions also often involved peers and teachers in managing breakdown situations, turning individual breakdown episodes into socially shared interactional events rather than isolated technical failures. The findings highlight how robot malfunctions become embedded within classroom interactional dynamics. This study contributes to research on classroom-based human–robot interaction by examining the ecological and sequential organization of robot breakdown episodes in naturalistic preschool settings.

candidates.title: Evaluating Social Reasoning in Embodied Vision-Language Models
candidates.abstract: Foundation models now serve as reasoning layers for robot teams, but it remains unclear whether embodiment-specialized vision-language models (VLMs) preserve the social-reasoning capabilities of general-purpose VLMs. We evaluate Gemini Robotics-ER on SHREC, a benchmark of real human-robot social interactions, and compare it with published general-purpose VLM baselines. Robotics-ER outperforms GPT-4o-mini on error/competence detection but performs worse on detailed social-attribute judgments; adding a visual frame helps one task while hurting the other. These results suggest embodiment-specialized models may perform differently on social judgments that can be read more directly from observable interaction cues versus those requiring more inference about a person's internal state. Because the comparison spans model families, these differences cannot be attributed to embodiment specialization alone. This matters for multi-robot systems, where a shared foundation model could cause systematic social-perception errors to influence multiple coordination decisions. This work presents an initial evaluation, with broader cross-context and video-based analyses left for future work.

candidates.title: Tiny Machine Learning for Smart Campus and Educational Applications
candidates.abstract: Advancing low-power real-time AI solutions on the edge, tiny machine learning (TinyML) transforms the educational environment. This chapter describes the embedding of Internet of Things (IoT) devices with TinyML functionalities in smart campuses, showcasing applications such as automated attendance systems, adaptive learning models, and plagiarism detection instruments powered by artificial intelligence (AI). Mobile learning applications can deliver tailored-made learning environments with very low power requirements through edge AI models. Efficiency and immediacy in plagiarism detection will help sustain the integrity of research when using TinyML. Here, some issues are discussed, the most dominant being hardware and data privacy constraints that must be overcome to deploy TinyML in educational organizations. It investigates emerging research areas that would benefit in completing this research. TinyML can go a long way in generating smart, sustainable, and AI-enabled schools.

candidates.title: Exploring AI Robot Mobility in Real Residential Environments for People Living with Frailty: An Observational Study
candidates.abstract: As policies increasingly promote assistive robots to support aging in place, little is known about whether real, lived-in homes can accommodate meaningful human–robot cohabitation for people living with frailty. This observational study examined how residential built environments shape such feasibility. Eight assisted-living residences in England (seven single-occupancy and one shared by a couple) were 3D scanned and reconstructed as CAD floor plans to simulate the movement of a commercially available humanoid robot (Pepper). Robot movement was fragmented in all residences because frailty-supporting adaptations, door widths, corridor constraints, and room geometry conflicted with robot clearance and sensing requirements. Critically, high-risk rooms were least accessible: no bedroom allowed full bed access (0/11), and bathrooms were inaccessible in 38% of residences, revealing a dual-user housing and robotics design challenge.

candidates.title: Dynamic identification and control issues for collaborative robots: the KUKA lightweight robot LWR 4+ case
candidates.abstract: Abstract Accurate dynamic models are essential for high-performance control, both for trajectory tracking and physical human–robot interaction involving collision detection, reaction, and force control. This work presents a comprehensive framework for dynamic modeling and identification of the KUKA LWR 4+ collaborative robot based on two complementary approaches. The first exploits signals provided by the KUKA Fast Research Interface, combined with nonlinear joint-friction identification to improve torque prediction. The second is a general methodology applicable to collaborative robots with or without joint elasticity. We present the first complete identification and experimental validation of the KUKA LWR 4+ dynamic model using our Penalty-Based Parameter Retrieval framework, demonstrating its ability to retrieve a physically consistent model for a collaborative robot with elastic joints. For the first time for this robot, the approach yields a complete physically consistent set of dynamic parameters suitable for Newton–Euler algorithms, simulation, and internal wrench estimation. The resulting model is compared with the KUKA LWR 4+ model available in CoppeliaSim, which relies on empirically estimated CAD-based parameters. A procedure is also proposed to incorporate an unknown payload without complete re-identification. Although the resulting model accurately captures the robot dynamics, its direct use in torque control requires accounting for the low-level torque loop, which only partially compensates for joint elasticity. A novel recursive least-squares algorithm is therefore proposed to compensate for this effect. Finally, the validated model is employed in sensorless collision detection, isolation, and reaction experiments, demonstrating its suitability for real-time interaction control.

candidates.title: Anthropomorphism in service robots and consumer acceptance: investigating the relationship via a systematic literature review
candidates.abstract: Purpose The purpose of this study is to investigate the effect of social robots anthropomorphism on consumers’ attitudes, acceptance and intention to use social robots. Design/methodology/approach A systematic literature review was conducted to a total of 96 articles that were selected from reputable scientific journals according to the Chartered Association of Business Schools (CABS) Journal Guide, published between 2015 and 2025. The TCCM (Theory-Content-Characteristic-Methodology) framework was used for data analysis, while a systematic content analysis was also performed. Findings The findings of the application of the TCCM framework highlight the most frequently used theories, research development frameworks, methodologies followed and research outcomes. In addition, it draws attention to the factors that act as moderators and mediators in the relationship between the anthropomorphism of social robots and the attitude, acceptance and intention to use them. Finally, the study concludes with recommendations for further research. Originality/value No literature review has examined all related literature on anthropomorphism attitude, acceptance and intention to use social robots.

candidates.title: Robots Do Not Arrive Empty-Handed
candidates.abstract: As robots increasingly enter care, health, and service environments, they do not arrive as neutral tools but as socio-material actors carrying historical inequalities and institutional biases. Mainstream human–robot interaction (HRI) often obscures these dynamics through laboratory-centered metrics and universalist assumptions about the “user.” This chapter introduces the Decolonial HRI Field Guide , a methodological framework designed to redistribute epistemic authority to communities affected by automation. Drawing on feminist STS, critical data studies, and participatory design, the guide operationalizes ethical reflection through two novel instruments: the Intersectional Reflexivity Log and the Data Governance Register. Through composite vignettes in healthcare and education, we demonstrate how these tools enable researchers to document positionality, negotiate contextual consent, and enforce community data sovereignty. This chapter concludes by arguing that ethical HRI requires moving beyond critique toward justiciable protocols that grant communities veto power over sensing and deployment.

candidates.title: Large language models combined with open-source algorithms for identifying prior art for obviousness analysis
candidates.abstract: The literature shows that patents often slow innovation, and patent parasites that patent commons innovation threaten the growth of entire industries, including additive manufacturing (AM) or 3D printing. AM has expanded through open-source hardware, software and shared material recipes, yet this cumulative innovation ecosystem is increasingly exposed to broad patents on AM materials. This article examines how obviousness doctrine should respond to algorithmic and large language model (LLM)-assisted prior-art generation in cumulative-innovation fields. Twenty-five U.S. AM materials patents and applications from 2016 to 2026 are mapped against an open-source algorithm for identifying obvious AM material prior art. The results suggest that many claims can be characterized as known printable material classes, predictable combinations of known feedstocks, routine additive use, or ordinary processing adaptations. The article argues that LLMs substantially reduces the difficulty of locating, parsing and applying prior art, providing a clear path for challenging obvious claims. A hybrid strategy is proposed as the strongest defense: deterministic, open-source databases for legally robust disclosure, combined with LLM-assisted claim parsing, semantic search and prioritization. Such systems could help patent examiners, researchers and open-source communities distinguish genuine inventions from predictable formulation work and preserve open access to the commons in many fields.

candidates.title: A Local Edge Companion Architecture for Human-Aware Communication and Service Augmentation in Cloud-Controlled Service Robots
candidates.abstract: Commercial cloud-controlled service robots are increasingly deployed in shared public facilities, yet many remain task-centric delivery platforms that cannot be easily extended with surrounding-people recognition, situated communication policy, or continuous access to internal middleware. This article proposes the Local Safety Companion Robot Extension (LSCRx), a non-invasive local edge companion architecture that augments such robots with human-aware communication while preserving manufacturer-controlled cloud operation and built-in safety functions. The central contribution is a communication-space design method that interprets robot–user distance, distance dynamics, body cues, field-of-view availability, and recognition confidence as service-level evidence. In the proposed conceptual policy, a gradual, confidence-supported decrease in distance would be treated as participation evidence, whereas separation, stopping outside the service zone, target loss, or unstable recognition would lead to waiting, distant greeting, information display, or other distance-preserving service actions. A prototype combines a commercial service robot with smartphone-class companion modules and a local edge server to demonstrate local body tracking, self-localization, data transmission, and cloud-API command preparation. Viewpoint-aware selection among registered spatial service waypoints (RSSWs) and anti-chasing rules are proposed as a conceptual model and were not implemented or evaluated in the present prototype. In the baseline route study, offline translational correction using known route-endpoint coordinates reduced the mean return-segment human-position error from 0.770 m to 0.476 m (approximately 38.2%) on the recorded data; this reduction was not independently validated. The evaluation was limited to one robot at a single university indoor location. Exploratory experiments involved seven participants, yielding six valid body-tracking datasets and seven questionnaire responses. These experiments and field observations suggest that contactless cues, camera placement, stop distance, and field of view jointly influence service usability under the tested conditions. The findings suggest a potential HRI design gap: the distance that is socially appropriate for a person may not coincide with the distance that is technically appropriate for reliable skeleton recognition. These preliminary findings further suggest that near-distance service interaction may benefit from both distance-aware robot policy and robust wide-field smartphone-based AR/body-tracking support that can preserve skeleton completeness and metric spatial stability. Further evaluation is needed to assess generalizability beyond this setting.

candidates.title: How Cognitive Apprenticeship Cultivates Computational Thinking in Young Learners: A Teacher–Student–Robot Triad in Educational Robotics
candidates.abstract: Computational thinking (CT) is a foundational competence for young learners, yet its abstract and algorithmic nature poses challenges in primary education. Educational robotics can support CT development, but the pedagogical processes and the robot’s role remain insufficiently understood. This chapter examines how cognitive apprenticeship (CA) methods and teacher techniques support children’s CT development and how the robot participates in this process. A mixed-methods case study with a qualitative emphasis investigated a four-week robotics summer camp involving 32 children aged seven to nine in southern China. Classroom observations, semi-structured interviews, and rubric-based scoring using a K–12 CT framework informed the analysis. Students’ CT scores improved significantly during the camp. The six CA methods foregrounded specific CT competences: cognitive modelling and coaching emphasised abstraction; scaffolding, logical reasoning; articulation and reflection, solution analysis and implementation; and exploration, generalisation and transfer. In human–robot interaction, the robot externalised students’ thinking, provided behavioural feedback on their programmes, and generated teachable moments during debugging. These interactions suggest a pedagogical triad in which the teacher scaffolds, the student programmes, and the robot makes students’ thinking observable. By detailing these processes, the chapter complements evidence of robotics’ effectiveness, conceptualises the robot as a cognitive partner, and offers educators concrete techniques for fostering CT in young learners.

candidates.title: A Two-Phase Fuzzy Quality Function Deployment Framework for Customer-Driven Intelligent Design of Hotel Service Robots
candidates.abstract: Abstract Service robots are increasingly deployed in hospitality environments, where successful design depends not only on mechanical and operational performance but also on context awareness, safe human–robot interaction, reliability, adaptive behavior, ethical AI, and user acceptance. However, early-stage design methods provide limited systematic support for translating subjective stakeholder requirements into prioritized intelligence-oriented design capabilities and corresponding enabling technologies (ETs) under uncertainty. This study proposes a two-phase fuzzy QFD framework in which CRs are first mapped to intelligent design attributes (IDAs), after which the resulting priorities are translated into ETs. Linguistic judgments are represented using triangular fuzzy numbers and defuzzified through graded mean integration representation. As prospective extensions, the study outlines CIDPI and ECC for future integration of multidimensional and ethical information; these constructs are not applied in the present case because their required inputs were not collected. The methodology is illustrated through an expert-based hotel service robot design case involving 22 participants from Fujian Province, China, including hotel managers, frequent hotel guests, robotics engineers, and AI ethics specialists. Within this demonstration context, context awareness and perception, safe human–robot interaction, and operational reliability emerged as the highest-priority IDAs, while AI-based perception and control, sensor fusion and autonomous navigation, and machine learning for adaptive behavior were the highest-priority ETs. Sensitivity analyses indicated that the dominant rankings remained stable within the predefined perturbation ranges. The proposed framework provides a traceable basis for linking stakeholder requirements with intelligent design priorities and technology-selection decisions during early-stage hotel service robot design.

candidates.title: LIBERO-PeRM: Benchmarking Personalized Robotic Manipulation
candidates.abstract: Personalization is essential for general-purpose robots to transition into household environments and achieve true practicality. While general robotic manipulation has been extensively studied, personalized robotic manipulation (PeRM) lacks a controlled benchmark for separating task completion from preference satisfaction. We introduce LIBERO-PeRM, a benchmark for preference learning in embodied agents. LIBERO-PeRM studies five questions: 1) how policies follow preferences in zero-shot settings; 2) how they learn single preferences from demonstrations; 3) how efficiently they acquire preferences as demonstrations increase; 4) how learned preferences generalize across layouts and tasks; and 5) how policies compose preferences and behave under conflicts. We propose a controlled formulation and taxonomy of observable preferences in simulation, covering motion, skill, and user-profile choices. This formulation is restricted to language-expressible preferences that can be instantiated in LIBERO without changing the task goal, evaluated automatically, and reused across tasks. Building on LIBERO, our procedural pipeline generates paired demonstrations with and without preferences. We create five task suites (312 tasks) with high-quality demonstrations, rich metadata, and preference-satisfaction metrics. Experiments show that current VLA policies struggle with zero-shot personalization, while SFT makes preferences learnable. Mixed training achieves better no-preference retention than sequential adaptation and improves performance with contextual prompts compared with preference-only training, but can weaken motion-preference learning; preference generalization, decomposition, and conflict handling remain difficult. The code, datasets, and demos can be found on the project website: https://libero-perm.github.io/.

candidates.title: Hardware Platforms for Tiny Machine Learning
candidates.abstract: Tiny machine learning (TinyML) is a rapidly growing field for deploying state-of-the-art machine learning models and algorithms in ultra-low-power hardware devices. These devices run on low memory, processing power, and energy. This chapter provides a comprehensive review of diverse hardware platforms that facilitate TinyML, detailing their architectures, computational performance, efficiency, energy efficiency, and everyday use cases. Details include a side-by-side comparison with the ARM Cortex-M, RISC-V processors, ESP32, and specialty accelerators such as Google's Edge TPU and NVIDIA's Jetson Nano. This chapter also addresses the trade-offs between performance and power consumption, highlights the specific challenges of this trade-off today, and discusses potential developments in TinyML hardware that could lead to improvements in the future.

candidates.title: A Sequential Approach to Realize Tiny Machine Learning in Hardware Platform
candidates.abstract: Tiny machine learning (TinyML) represents a transformative frontier in artificial intelligence, enabling the deployment of machine learning models on resource-constrained devices. This technology embeds deep learning capabilities directly into billions of Internet of Things (IoT) devices and microcontrollers (MCUs), significantly expanding the scope of intelligent applications while enabling ubiquitous computing at the extreme edge. The implementation of TinyML presents substantial challenges due to severe hardware limitations, such as memory constraints, processing capabilities, and power requirements. These constraints were the motivations that led to the development of specialized processor architecture integrated in various hardware platforms designed specifically to support machine learning models for forecasting. This chapter comprehensively examines the current landscape of hardware platforms for TinyML implementations, analyzing their architectures, capabilities, and performance characteristics.

candidates.title: Power Management in Tiny Machine Learning
candidates.abstract: Tiny machine learning (TinyML) is transforming intelligent applications by allowing machine learning inference directly on resource-constrained edge devices. Because the majority of TinyML systems will operate in environments with limited battery life or energy harvesting, managing the power of such systems will play a significant role in the success or failure of their intended applications. In this chapter, we provide a detailed account of power management in TinyML systems, starting with the need and challenges presented by power-constrained environments. We explore energy-harvesting methods that allow devices to operate, and we provide strategies for managing and optimizing power consumption. Next, we discuss power profiling at both hardware and software layers, identifying the primary sources of energy usage and suggesting techniques for power-aware profiling. The chapter also focuses on energy-efficient machine learning models (including low-power neural architectures) and energy-aware software tools that decrease total consumption. We discuss the multitude of optimization techniques in hardware, software, operating systems, and hybrid (hardware/software) solutions that improve system lifetime without compromising performance. To show real-world examples of power-efficient TinyML applications, we provide several relevant case studies. Finally, we suggest future research directions and emphasize the need for adaptive, context-aware power management methods. This will provide valuable insights for researchers and practitioners developing sustainable design methods for low-power intelligent systems on the edge.

candidates.title: Analysis of Model Compression Techniques for Tiny Machine Learning
candidates.abstract: This chapter explores tiny machine learning (TinyML) as a means to help compress machine learning (ML) models for deployment on memory-constrained hardware. Two case studies provide different approaches to developing efficient and compact models capable of being deployed on the edge. The first case study focused on a specific type of acoustic scene classification (ASC) with a defined subset of the Acoustic Scenes dataset, simplifying the task from multiclass classification to binary classification (i.e., identifying the presence of sound vs. not identifying the presence of sound). In this case study, several models were tested, including bilayered neural networks, linear discriminant analysis, subspace discriminant, linear support vector machines (SVM), and logistic regression. It also demonstrated model compression through feature selection with the minimum-redundancy maximum-relevance (MRMR) algorithm, quantized models, and models optimized with memory-aware Bayesian hyperparameter optimization methods. Results show that models such as linear SVM and logistic regression could achieve model sizes below 30 KB while retaining classification accuracy levels up to 86%. Additionally, doubling the number of features from 25 to 50 improved performance and reduced model size. For example, the Bilayered NN_5 model improved performance accuracy from 31% to 82.67%, and a new model size of even less than 10 KB. The results display the potential for deploying TinyML to support intelligent systems on devices with limited memory resources, such as hearing aids. Image classification is considered with a focus on deploying a deep learning model on embedded platforms like Raspberry Pi, in case study 2. This method uses transfer learning using the CIFAR-10 dataset. The authors use a two-stage compression pipeline consisting of filter pruning based on Taylor-based importance scoring and 8-bit quantization. After the pruning is complete, the authors fine-tune the pruned models to recover performance. The authors also used post-training quantization techniques to reduce the memory requirement and inference time of the model, which could be used at the edge.

candidates.title: Embedded Systems and Internet of Things Foundations
candidates.abstract: The convergence of embedded systems and the Internet of Things (IoT) has accelerated the development of tiny machine learning (TinyML) real-time intelligence, which is delivered on ultra-low-power devices. Thus, this chapter examines the architecture, design methodologies, and emerging roles of embedded systems within the broader IoT ecosystem. This chapter provides a foundational understanding of embedded systems, establishing the components and structures of embedded systems, putting embedded system architectures into the context of IoT architectures, and understanding the increasing roles of embedded systems in improving intelligent edge computing. A detailed examination of embedded architectures, real-time operating systems, and performance limitations provided discourses on the trade-offs designers face between the outcome of embedded systems for real-world applications and the intentional consequences of designs. In the architectural context of IoT, smart services will realise their full potential when they leverage reliable, communicating sensors and actuators included in their design, and direct human intervention at the history collection void. A closer examination of the IoT architecture with its layers opened up communication protocols with embedded sensors and actuators, which are the main drivers combining the edges to connect. Considering the context of embedded IoT, the editors analyzed data processing, secure communication, and deployment to the real world. Based on this discussion of traditional embodied intelligence, the chapter will consider IoT and the challenges of deploying artificial intelligence (AI) as a service, and review the literature in which academic researchers and industry organizations are engaged in deploying TinyML on constrained hardware. A focused discussion follows on how embedded platforms facilitate the execution of machine learning models, with considerations for tools such as TensorFlow Lite Micro. Design methodologies are analyzed and critiqued with a focus on the principles of hardware-software co-design, performance optimization, and real-time processing. A subset of the findings employed in this chapter is based on benchmarking studies and inference-time analysis performed across a wide range of microcontroller platforms. Finally, examples have been provided with an application focus ranging from smart homes, industrial automation, and healthcare to show how the trends are being harnessed. Future directions of the field, namely sustainable edge AI, interoperability, and on-device learning, are provided before concluding. This chapter illustrates that embedded systems and IoT represent the foundation for the next generation of intelligent systems.

candidates.title: Yeah Hand v1.3: an open source tendon-driven robotic and prosthetic hand
candidates.abstract: Open source anthropomorphic hand, 3D-printable, usable as a robotic end effector and as an active prosthetic hand. Successor of Rebelia V1 (OSHWA certified IT000021, DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23394100). Five serial bus servomotors housed in the internal skeleton of the hand drive the fingers through antagonistic flexion and extension tendons. Each tendon end runs in its own PTFE Bowden tube, seated in holes, tunnels and slots of the skeleton, to a two-part spool (flexion part and extension part) on the actuator flange. Ring and little fingers are coupled directly on the same spool. The thumb rotation servo, with the thumb base on its flange, is mounted on a removable platform. The ESP32 firmware provides whole-hand calibration, force-limited grasps, grasp presets, a ROS mode streaming position, load, voltage, temperature and current of every actuator, and two-channel FFT-based EMG control in the prosthetic version. Published as open source hardware and as a public technical disclosure (prior art). First published on GitHub on 26 November 2025 as Rebelia V2, i.e. Yeah Hand v1.0 (opsobot/rebelia, branch V2) Hardware: CERN-OHL-S-2.0. Firmware: GPL-3.0-or-later. Documentation and images: CC-BY-SA-4.0. "Yeah Hand" is a registered EU trademark (no. 019374244).

candidates.title: Yeah Hand (formerly Rebelia): an open source tendon-driven robotic and prosthetic hand
candidates.abstract: Open source anthropomorphic hand, fully 3D-printable, usable as a robotic end effector and as an active prosthetic hand. Five serial bus servomotors housed in the internal skeleton of the hand drive the fingers through antagonistic flexion and extension tendons wound in opposite directions on one spool per actuator. Ring and little fingers share one actuator through a sliding tendon loop that lets them adapt to the object. The thumb base is mounted directly on the output flange of the thumb rotation actuator. The ESP32-based firmware performs load-based tendon calibration at start-up, force-limited grasps and grasp presets controlled by a single closure value. In the prosthetic version, two surface EMG channels are processed by FFT and compared with two intensity thresholds to open, close or hold the hand; the grasp can be selected by rotating the unpowered thumb by hand. This record contains the complete design files (CAD, STL, electronic board, firmware) and documentation. It is published as open source hardware and as a public technical disclosure (prior art). First public disclosure on GitHub: 3 March 2025. Hardware: CERN-OHL-S-2.0. Firmware: GPL-3.0-or-later. Documentation and images: CC-BY-SA-4.0. "Yeah Hand" is a registered EU trademark.

candidates.title: Let Me Look at You: Advanced Facial Expression Modeling for Conversational Speech Synthesis
candidates.abstract: Conversational Speech Synthesis (CSS) is a fundamental component of human-computer interaction, aiming to generate contextually appropriate, expressive, and empathetic speech. However, facial expressions encode subtle and rich affective cues that are crucial for empathetic speech interaction, whereas existing approaches often overlook this important modality. In addition, the lack of large-scale natural conversational datasets with both speech and visual modalities also limits the development of visual affect understanding in conversational settings. To address these limitations, we propose FacialTalker, a facial-expression-aware CSS framework built upon a large language model backbone. To efficiently encode facial expressions, we propose AUTokenizer, a single-codebook visual tokenizer that discretizes each frame-level facial expression into a compact token, trained with supervision from combinations of facial Action Units. We further introduce a dual direct preference optimization (DualDPO) strategy, which extends the DPO by jointly imposing preference constraints on both visual and speech token sequences, to enhance the model's understanding of facial expressions and speech semantics in multimodal conversational contexts. Moreover, we construct VSDD-1K, a large-scale multimodal dialogue dataset collected through a fully automated pipeline from real-world Internet conversations, comprising over 1,033 hours of synchronized speaker videos and speech, with more than 85% of frames containing valid faces. Extensive objective and subjective experiments demonstrate that FacialTalker consistently outperforms strong baselines in facial-expression perception and speech synthesis quality, generating speech that is more natural, expressive, and better aligned with the conversational context. The results also validate the effectiveness of our training strategy and dataset construction pipeline. The project page: https://github.com/walker-hyf/FacialTalker.
